title: Lakehouse-to-Power-BI BI serving over OneLake with Direct Lake
purpose: Show how interactive Power BI reports are served from a Fabric lakehouse over OneLake using a Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model, and how a single Fabric F-SKU capacity underpins and bounds the whole read path.
accessibleSummary: A read-path architecture diagram. Power BI report visuals live-connect to a Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model and issue DAX. The model lazily loads only the columns a query touches, straight from the lakehouse's curated gold Delta tables on OneLake, and keeps recently used columns resident in capacity memory to serve later queries. A framing operation rebinds the model to the latest Delta commit as a metadata-only step. A residency panel shows the cold/semiwarm/warm/hot states. A warning band flags that exceeding the SKU memory bound causes cold reads from OneLake at peak and that OneSecurity on the source lakehouse can force a DirectQuery fallback. A capacity band at the bottom shows the single F-SKU that sets the per-model memory bound, gates free-license report viewing at F64, and smooths interactive spikes.
longDescription: This diagram grounds a common BI-serving decision in Microsoft Fabric: reporting over a lakehouse without a second copy or a refresh pipeline. The lakehouse persists one physical Delta/Parquet copy of its curated gold tables on OneLake, which every Fabric engine reads. A Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model binds to those tables and, on query, lazily loads only the columns the DAX query touches — plus those needed by relationships and measures — directly from OneLake, retaining recently accessed columns in an in-memory cache to serve subsequent queries. That residency sits in one of four states (cold, semiwarm, warm, hot), and a resident column is evicted by a framing operation, prolonged non-use, or capacity memory pressure. Framing itself is a metadata-only rebind to the latest Delta commit version that typically finishes in seconds, so freshness tracks the lakehouse writes without a scheduled refresh. Every element — Spark writes, OneLake reads, the semantic model's memory, and report DAX — draws Capacity Units from a single Fabric F-SKU capacity. That SKU sets the per-model Direct Lake memory bound, so under-sizing surfaces as cold reads from OneLake at peak rather than an outright failure; F64 is separately the licensing threshold above which free-license users can view reports. Interactive report queries smooth over a 5-to-64-minute window and compound-throttling protection charges a fan-out request (visual to model to OneLake) at most once. A warning band isolates the two failure modes this design must plan for: overshooting the memory bound, and enabling OneSecurity on the source lakehouse, which is reported to push the model into DirectQuery fallback.

nodes.label: Report visuals
nodes.summary: Power BI report visuals live-connect to the published semantic model and issue DAX queries; no data is copied into the report.
nodes.detail: Reports are built on the published semantic model over a live connection, so the report is authored and edited without changing the model itself; at least Build permission on the model is required to live-connect. Each visual emits a DAX query against the model. Because Direct Lake keeps no separate cache in the report and imports nothing, the report layer holds no data copy of its own.
nodes.whyItMatters: The report layer being a thin live-connected client is what lets many reports share one governed semantic model, and it keeps the freshness and sizing decisions concentrated in the model and capacity below rather than scattered across report files.

evidence.note: Reports built on a published semantic model use a live connection, so the report can be authored and edited without changing the model itself; at least Build permission on the model is required to live-connect.
Direct Lake mode, available to Power BI through Fabric, lets reports query data sitting in OneLake directly, without importing it into the model or maintaining a separate cache.

inputs: An end user opening a report page, which triggers each visual to request its data
processing: Each visual generates a DAX query
The query is sent over the live connection to the published semantic model
outputs: Rendered visuals populated from the model's query results
drill.example: A sales dashboard's 12 visuals each emit a DAX query on page load; all resolve against the same live-connected Direct Lake model with no data copied into the .pbix.
controls: Build permission granted to report authors
Report-level measures defined without writing into the shared model
failureModes: Authoring a local Import/DirectQuery model bundled with the report instead of live-connecting, which reintroduces a copy and a refresh

nodes.label: Direct Lake on OneLake semantic model
nodes.summary: Reads Delta columns straight from OneLake, lazily loading only what a query touches; never falls back to DirectQuery.
nodes.detail: A Direct Lake semantic model loads column data from OneLake lazily: nothing is read until a query first touches a column, and the load set includes not just the columns the query names but also those needed by relationships and measures. When a report visual requests data, the model reads the Delta table in OneLake directly and may retain recently accessed data in an in-memory cache to serve subsequent queries efficiently. Direct Lake on OneLake never falls back to DirectQuery and skips SQL-endpoint coupling entirely, which enables more efficient DAX query plans since no SQL security check is needed. The model is anchored to a Delta commit version by framing.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the component that delivers the design's core promise — import-like query performance over data that currently sits in the lakehouse, with no refresh job to build or fail — and choosing the OneLake flavor keeps the query path simplest and fastest.

evidence.note: Direct Lake is a semantic-model storage mode in which the model reads Delta tables straight from OneLake, avoiding both data import and DirectQuery, and so pairs import-like performance with DirectQuery-like freshness.

Direct Lake loads column data from OneLake lazily: nothing is read until a query first touches a column, and the load set includes columns needed by relationships and measures. Direct Lake on OneLake never falls back to DirectQuery and skips SQL-endpoint coupling, enabling more efficient DAX query plans.

When a report visual requests data from a Direct Lake table, the semantic model reads the Delta table in OneLake directly and may retain recently accessed data in an in-memory cache to serve subsequent queries efficiently.

inputs: A DAX query from a report visual naming certain columns/measures
processing: Determine the full column load set (named columns plus relationship and measure dependencies)
Load any not-yet-resident columns lazily from the framed OneLake Delta files
Answer the query and retain the loaded columns in the in-memory cache
outputs: Query result to the visual; warmed resident columns for the next query
drill.example: A visual grouping revenue by region loads the region, revenue, and the relationship key columns on first use; a follow-up visual filtering the same region reuses those now-resident columns.
controls: Direct Lake flavor choice (OneLake vs SQL) — OneLake is the recommended default here
Automatic-updates setting governing when framing runs
failureModes: Choosing Direct Lake on SQL and basing a table on a SQL view, forcing every query into DirectQuery fallback
OneSecurity on the source lakehouse reportedly forcing fallback

nodes.label: Curated gold Delta tables
nodes.summary: One physical Delta/Parquet copy of the reporting tables in the lakehouse Tables area on OneLake.
nodes.detail: A lakehouse's managed tables use the Delta Lake storage format over Parquet, and all Fabric data items persist their tabular data in OneLake as open Delta Parquet regardless of which engine wrote it. That one-copy design lets multiple Fabric engines operate over the same physical Delta Parquet data, so reporting reads the same files Spark wrote without a second copy. For Direct Lake specifically, these tables are written V-Ordered, with a ~1 GB Optimized Write file target and low-cardinality partitions so column loads stay cheap.
nodes.whyItMatters: The single physical copy on OneLake is the architectural foundation that makes copy-free reporting possible; the write-side layout choices here directly determine how fast the Direct Lake model can transcode and load columns above.

evidence.note: All managed lakehouse tables use the Delta Lake storage format, which supplies ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel over the underlying Parquet files.

All Fabric data items automatically persist their tabular data in OneLake using the open Delta Parquet format regardless of engine, and the one-copy design lets multiple Fabric engines operate over the same physical Delta Parquet data.

A 1 GB BinSize target is recommended when writing Delta tables that back Power BI Direct Lake semantic models, because larger files align with the Direct Lake loading pattern and reduce the number of segment loads needed.

Partition Delta tables only on low-cardinality columns (Microsoft suggests under about 100-200 distinct values); over-partitioning multiplies small files and row groups, inflating segment counts in the model.

inputs: Curated, modelled gold data produced by upstream Spark/SQL transformation
processing: Write as Delta into the lakehouse Tables area
Apply V-Order and a ~1 GB Optimized Write target
outputs: Report-ready Delta tables on OneLake that the Direct Lake model binds to
drill.example: A gold FactSales table is written V-Ordered with a 1 GB bin size and partitioned by sales_region (12 values), keeping its row-group and segment counts favourable for Direct Lake loading.
controls: V-Order enablement for these read-heavy tables
failureModes: Overwrite loads wiping commit history and forcing full cold reloads
Over-partitioning on a high-cardinality column, inflating segment counts and slowing queries

nodes.label: Column residency
nodes.summary: The model occupies cold, semiwarm, warm, or hot memory states; latency improves at each step, bounded by SKU memory.
nodes.detail: A Direct Lake model occupies one of four memory-residency states — cold, semiwarm, warm, or hot — with query latency improving at each step; hot adds populated VertiScan caches on top of fully resident column data. A resident column can be evicted for three reasons: a framing operation after the source Delta table changed, prolonged non-use by queries, or general memory pressure on the capacity from concurrent operations. On a cold query the engine must transcode columns from OneLake, which is why the write-side layout of the gold tables matters.
nodes.whyItMatters: Whether reports feel fast is largely a question of how much of the model stays hot; that in turn depends on the SKU memory bound and on concurrent load, making residency the bridge between the model and the capacity below.

evidence.note: A Direct Lake model occupies one of four memory-residency states — cold, semiwarm, warm, or hot — with query latency improving at each step; hot adds populated VertiScan caches on top of fully resident column data.

A resident column can be evicted for three reasons: a framing operation after the source Delta table changed, prolonged non-use by queries, or general memory pressure on the capacity from concurrent operations.

inputs: Queries arriving against columns in varying residency states
processing: Cold: transcode the needed columns from OneLake Parquet into in-memory VertiPaq format
Hot: serve from resident columns plus populated VertiScan caches
outputs: Query results whose latency depends on the starting residency state
drill.example: The first query of the morning hits cold columns and transcodes them; by mid-morning the frequently used columns are hot and queries return at import-like speed.
controls: SKU memory bound (how much can stay resident)
Concurrency on the capacity (memory pressure evicts columns)
failureModes: Frequent eviction from memory pressure keeping the model perpetually cold/semiwarm
A large framing operation dropping the model back to cold at a busy time

nodes.label: Failure modes to design around
nodes.summary: Overshooting the SKU memory bound causes cold reads at peak; OneSecurity on the source lakehouse can force DirectQuery fallback.
nodes.detail: Two failure modes shape this design. First, the Fabric capacity SKU sets the maximum memory available to each Direct Lake semantic model, which bounds how much column data can be resident at once; overshooting it surfaces as on-demand cold reads from OneLake at peak, a degradation rather than an outright error. Second, community reporting indicates that enabling OneLake data-access roles (OneSecurity) on the same lakehouse a Direct Lake model is built on can push the model into DirectQuery fallback — so RLS placement and OneSecurity must be verified against this design before rollout.
nodes.whyItMatters: Both failure modes are silent-ish — the design keeps working but slower — so they must be designed against up front (through sizing and a security-placement decision) rather than discovered under production load.

evidence.note: The Fabric capacity SKU sets the maximum memory available to each Direct Lake semantic model, which bounds how much column data can be resident at once.

OneLake data access roles (OneSecurity) are described as incompatible with Direct Lake semantic models built on the same Lakehouse: enabling OneSecurity can cause the model to drop out of Direct Lake mode. (Tier-6 community source — treat as verify-before-relying.)

inputs: A model whose resident footprint approaches the SKU bound, or a lakehouse where OneSecurity is being considered
processing: Under memory pressure, columns that don't fit are read on demand (cold) from OneLake
If OneSecurity is enabled on the source lakehouse, queries reportedly fall back to DirectQuery
outputs: Degraded query latency at peak, or a mode change to DirectQuery
drill.example: A model sized just under an F-SKU bound runs fine off-peak but hits cold reads during the Monday-morning concurrency spike; separately, a security team enabling OneSecurity on the source lakehouse is reported to knock the model out of Direct Lake mode.
controls: SKU right-sizing with headroom for concurrency
Deciding RLS/OneSecurity placement (semantic-model layer vs OneLake) before go-live
failureModes: Sizing to average without headroom, so peak concurrency triggers cold reads
Enabling OneSecurity on the source lakehouse without testing Direct Lake behaviour first

nodes.label: OneLake
nodes.summary: The single logical data lake holding one physical Delta/Parquet copy that every Fabric engine reads.
nodes.detail: Every Fabric tenant is provisioned with exactly one OneLake, and all Fabric data items persist their tabular data there in the open Delta Parquet format regardless of which engine wrote it. The one-copy design lets T-SQL, Spark, Analysis Services, and others operate over the same physical Delta Parquet data — which is precisely what lets the Direct Lake model read the lakehouse's gold tables with no second copy.
nodes.whyItMatters: OneLake being a single shared copy is the reason this architecture avoids the import/refresh cycle entirely: reporting reads the same files ETL wrote.

evidence.note: Every Microsoft Fabric tenant is provisioned with exactly one OneLake; all Fabric data items persist tabular data in OneLake as open Delta Parquet regardless of engine, and the one-copy design lets multiple Fabric engines operate over the same physical data.

inputs: Delta Parquet files written by the lakehouse's transformation jobs
processing: Store one physical copy per table under the workspace/item namespace
Serve reads to any Fabric engine over the same files
outputs: The single source the Direct Lake model reads from
drill.example: The gold FactSales files written by a Spark job are the identical files the Direct Lake model transcodes columns from — no copy step between them.
failureModes: Standing up separate physical lakes per team, reintroducing duplication OneLake exists to avoid

nodes.label: Single Fabric F-SKU capacity
nodes.summary: One CU pool backs the whole path; the SKU sets the per-model memory bound, gates F64 free-license viewing, and smooths spikes.
nodes.detail: A Fabric capacity is a dedicated pool of resources measured in Capacity Units, and F SKUs run F2 to F2048 with the SKU number equalling its CUs and each step doubling compute. That SKU sets the maximum memory available to each Direct Lake semantic model. F64 is the licensing threshold for broad report consumption: on F64 or larger, free-license users can view reports with a workspace viewer role. Interactive operations smooth over 5 to 64 minutes, and compound throttling protection charges a fan-out request (report visual → semantic model → OneLake) at most once, so size for sustained load rather than peak.
nodes.whyItMatters: This single capacity is simultaneously the memory bound for the model, the licensing gate for who can view reports, and the throttling boundary for the workload — which is why SKU selection here is the design's biggest cost/performance lever.

evidence.note: Fabric F SKUs run from F2 up to F2048, the SKU number equals its capacity units (F64 = 64 CUs), and each step doubles compute. On F64 or larger, free-license users can view Power BI content with a workspace viewer role, whereas smaller SKUs require paid seats.
The Fabric capacity SKU sets the maximum memory available to each Direct Lake semantic model, which bounds how much column data can be resident at once.

Interactive operations are smoothed over a minimum of 5 minutes and up to 64 minutes; compound throttling protection charges a fan-out request (a report visual querying a semantic model that reads from OneLake) at most once.

inputs: The expected model footprint, concurrency, and report audience size
processing: Pick an F-SKU whose memory bound holds the resident model with headroom
Raise the floor to F64 if broad free-license viewing is required
Rely on smoothing/bursting to absorb short interactive spikes
outputs: A single capacity that backs Spark writes, OneLake reads, the model, and report queries
drill.example: A team picks F64 because 400 free-license users must view the reports, even though the model itself would fit a smaller SKU on memory — licensing sets the floor, not compute.
controls: Whether heavy Spark/ETL shares this capacity or gets its own
failureModes: Sizing purely on memory and forgetting the F64 licensing floor
Co-locating heavy ETL on the same capacity and starving report memory at peak

edges.label: framing rebinds model to latest Delta commit
SKU sets the per-model memory bound

walkthrough.title: Start: a report visual asks for data
walkthrough.explanation: Reports live-connect to the published semantic model and each visual emits a DAX query — nothing is imported or cached in the report itself.

walkthrough.title: The model reads columns straight from OneLake
walkthrough.explanation: The Direct Lake on OneLake model lazily loads only the columns the query touches (plus relationship/measure dependencies) from the framed Delta files, and never takes a DirectQuery round trip.

walkthrough.title: The source is one physical copy of the gold tables
walkthrough.explanation: The lakehouse's curated gold Delta tables — written V-Ordered with ~1 GB files and low-cardinality partitions — are the single copy the model reads, with no second dataset to refresh.

walkthrough.title: OneLake holds that one copy for every engine
walkthrough.explanation: Because all Fabric items persist Delta Parquet in OneLake, the model reads the same files the transformation jobs wrote — the basis for copy-free reporting.

walkthrough.title: Residency decides how fast queries feel
walkthrough.explanation: Columns move through cold/semiwarm/warm/hot states; hot columns give import-like latency, and eviction from framing, non-use, or memory pressure pushes them back toward cold.

walkthrough.title: Two failure modes to design around
walkthrough.explanation: Exceeding the SKU memory bound produces cold reads from OneLake at peak, and OneSecurity on the source lakehouse can force DirectQuery fallback — both to be handled by sizing and a security-placement decision up front.

walkthrough.title: One capacity bounds and meters all of it
walkthrough.explanation: A single F-SKU sets the model's memory bound, gates free-license report viewing at F64, and smooths interactive spikes — making SKU selection the design's central cost/performance decision.
